name: David Novak

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for seeing me, David. I'm a researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no links to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything here is confidential. Could you tell me about a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work for Brightwell Care, a private firm in town, and I mostly do the double-up calls, the heavier clients who need two of us and a hoist. I'm paired with Steve, who's been doing it twelve years and still corrects how I fold the sling. We do mornings from half six to eleven, a break, then the bedtime calls from five to nine. I used to be a gym instructor until the gym shut, so I'm strong, but I'm still learning the care side, the skin checks and the medicines. What I like is that it's real work and people need you. What wears me out is the split shift, you never get a proper day.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: And how about home, and things like phones and tech?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I live with my partner Lena, she's a dental nurse, in a one-bed flat I bought with help from my parents. So no rent, just a small mortgage, and we've got savings, more than a year of bills really. Tech, I avoid. I use the Brightwell app because I have to tap in and out of each call, but I've never used one of those AI chat things and I don't see why I would. Lena laughs at me for it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Here's the card: "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say fair enough, I never believed it anyway. At work with Steve I'd say nothing changes then, same hoist, same clients. I'm not online much, so I wouldn't post.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it suits me fine. I don't want things changing, I've only just got used to this job. Money's fine, the flat's nearly ours, Lena's job is steady.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing my double-ups with Steve. I'd keep paying extra off the mortgage, about three hundred a month. Maybe I'd finally do the medication course Brightwell keeps offering, because I'm weak on that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Relieved, if anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's one thing about the job you wish would change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The split shift. If I could do one block, I'd have afternoons with Lena. Nobody needs a robot to fix care, they need someone to sort out the split shift so carers see daylight with their families.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work keeps you going?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Steve, definitely. He's patient with me and tells stories about every client. If he ever left I'd probably think about leaving too.

say: I'd tell Steve **nothing changes**: same **hoist**, same clients.
I'd say I **never believed** the AI talk anyway.
think: It **suits me**, because I've only just got used to this job.
With the **flat** nearly paid and Lena's steady job, money is fine.
do: Pay about **three hundred** extra a month off the mortgage.
Take Brightwell's **medication course** to fix a weak spot.
S0.quote: Nobody needs a robot to fix care, they need someone to sort out the split shift so carers see daylight with their families.
fieldNote: His real complaint is the **split shift**, not technology.
He is anchored by **Steve**, his more experienced partner.
A nearly paid **flat** gives him an unusually strong position for a junior carer.

steps.text: Keep the morning and bedtime double-up calls with Steve
Pay three hundred a month extra off the flat mortgage
Sign up for Brightwell's medication course

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Here's the card: "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it doesn't touch us much, we're lifting people, not typing. Maybe the office gets smaller. I'd keep it low-key at work, I'm not one to make speeches.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think I'm fine for now. The robots are slow, and nobody is getting a sixteen-stone man out of bed with a machine soon. The bit that worries me is if the app gets more complicated and I'm the one who can't work it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on as normal and keep paying off the flat. If Brightwell brought in a new system, I'd do the training but I'd ask Steve or Lena to help me through it. I wouldn't go looking for anything new myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly calm. A bit uneasy about the app.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd ask Lena for help. Has that happened before?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, when the new app came in last year, she set it all up on my phone. My partner Lena set up the work app on my phone, because I'd have thrown it in the canal otherwise.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about the office staff at Brightwell?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: There are four of them doing rosters and the phones. I'd feel bad if they went, but it's a business, it has to make money. I'd hope they find something.

say: I'd say AI barely touches us, because we're **lifting people**, not typing.
I'd keep it **low-key** and maybe mention a smaller **office**.
think: My **hands-on** work is safe while robots stay slow.
My worry is a more complicated **app** that I can't work.
do: Carry on as **normal** and keep paying off the flat.
Do Brightwell's **training** with help from Steve or Lena.
feel: Mostly **calm**, a bit **uneasy** about the app.
S1.quote: My partner Lena set up the work app on my phone, because I'd have thrown it in the canal otherwise.
fieldNote: He leans on **Lena** for anything technical.
His centrist view treats office job losses as **business** reality.
He sees **heavy lifting** as his protection in this picture.

steps.text: Keep doing double-up hoist calls on the Brightwell rota
Keep overpaying the flat mortgage each month
Wait for Brightwell's new system and learn it with Lena's help

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Here's the card: "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's mad, and someone should slow it down, the government or whoever. At work I'd say let's see what happens, because Steve would say the same. I wouldn't go to protests.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truly, it worries me. AGI in two years means the office and the rotas are all computer by 2028, and then robots that can lift by 2031. Lifting is exactly my job, and I'd be thirty-two with no qualifications. The flat's a comfort, but I'd still need a wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop the extra mortgage payments and build up cash in the bank instead, so we've got it to hand. I'd wait a bit to see what Brightwell does, because they'd still need people until the robots are cheap. I might look at something like a porter job at the hospital, still physical, but I don't know.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. A knot in my stomach.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd wait. How long would you wait?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably too long, if I'm honest. I'd wait until Brightwell told me something. I'm the kind who stays until the lights go off, and with robots coming in 2031 that's not clever.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Lena say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She'd tell me to do a course now, while there's time. Dentistry might be safer for her, it's fiddly work in people's mouths. She'd probably end up carrying us for a bit if I lost my job.

say: I'd say it's **mad** and someone, maybe the **government**, should slow it down.
At work I'd say **let's see**, like Steve would.
think: Robots that can lift by **2031** go straight at my job.
The **flat** comforts me, but I'd still need a **wage**.
do: Stop **mortgage overpayments** and keep cash in the bank.
Maybe look at a hospital **porter** job.
S2.quote: I'm the kind who stays until the lights go off, and with robots coming in 2031 that's not clever.
fieldNote: He knows his **waiting** habit is risky here, and says so.
**Lifting** was his protection and becomes his exposure by 2031.
Lena's steadier income is his real **safety net**.

steps.text: Stop mortgage overpayments and keep the cash in savings
Wait for Brightwell's plans before making any move
Look at hospital porter vacancies on the local hospital jobs page

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Here's the card: "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's time, so let's not panic. At work I'd say we'd better get some qualifications in. I'd probably just say that to Steve.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think five years means I'd still have work until about 2034. The office goes in 2031, but lifting and washing last three years more. I'd be thirty-five, which feels old to start again, but it's not really.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the medication course and maybe the level 3 care certificate, because more skills means I'm the last to go. I'd keep the cash savings and keep a small mortgage overpayment. I'd keep an eye out for jobs in places like hospitals.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Still worried, but less. More of a dull ache.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said more skills means you're last to go. Is that what you believe?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think so. If they keep a few people to check on the robots, they'll keep the ones with certificates. In five years I could go from the new guy who folds the sling wrong to the one they keep.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you spend less on?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not much, we don't spend a lot. Maybe the car, I'd keep the old one longer. We'd skip the big holiday Lena wants.

say: I'd say there's **time** to prepare, so let's not panic about it.
I'd tell Steve we'd better get some **qualifications** in.
think: I'd keep work until about **2034**, when robots reach lifting.
Starting again at **thirty-five** feels old, but isn't really.
do: Take the **medication course** and the level 3 care certificate.
Keep **cash savings** and a small mortgage overpayment.
S3.quote: In five years I could go from the new guy who folds the sling wrong to the one they keep.
fieldNote: Five years moves him from waiting to **getting certificates**.
He believes skills will make him **last to go**, not safe for good.
He would cut the **holiday** before touching savings.

steps.text: Take the medication course and level 3 care certificate
Keep a cash savings pot alongside small mortgage overpayments
Skip the big holiday and keep the old car longer

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Here's the card: "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is ages, there's no point worrying yet. At work I'd say carry on. I'd probably joke that I'll be bald by then anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truly, I think I'd still be in care for most of the decade. By 2039 I'd be thirty-seven, and the flat would be paid off by then. That makes a big difference, if there's no mortgage I can take a smaller wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on, do the courses slowly, and keep paying off the flat. I'd wait and see what happens around 2036 with the office stuff before making any big move. Lena and I might think about kids in a few years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty calm, a bit uneasy at the back of my mind.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said a paid-off flat lets you take a smaller wage. What kind of job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anything steady, maybe a caretaker at a school or something with my hands. Once the flat's paid off, I can take any honest job and still sleep at night.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you tell Steve to do anything?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Steve's older, he'd be near sixty by then. I'd tell him to keep going, he'd probably retire right about when the robots turn up. Lucky him, really.

say: I'd say **ten years** is ages, so no point worrying yet.
I'd joke I'll be **bald** by then anyway.
think: I'd stay in care for most of the **decade**.
A **paid-off flat** by 2039 lets me take a smaller wage.
do: Do the **courses** slowly and keep paying off the flat.
Talk with Lena about **kids** in a few years.
feel: Pretty **calm**, with a bit of **unease** at the back of my mind.
S4.quote: Once the flat's paid off, I can take any honest job and still sleep at night.
fieldNote: The **mortgage-free** flat is his main plan, more than any new skill.
He returns to **waiting** once time feels plentiful.
He sees Steve as **lucky** to retire as robots arrive.

steps.text: Stay on Brightwell's double-up rota through the decade
Hold off on any job change until AGI arrives in 2036

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because the robots would come for the lifting by 2031 and I'd still be waiting for Brightwell to tell me something. What would help is a proper heads-up from the firm and a paid course I can do while still working.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about the clients' families. They're the ones who'll pick robots or people. The families choose the care, and if a robot is half the price, most of them will choose the robot and feel bad about it.

headlineQuote: The families choose the care, and if a robot is half the price, most of them will choose the robot and feel bad about it.
portrait: David is a **27-year-old** former gym instructor doing heavy **double-up calls** for a private firm.
He owns a small **flat** with help from his parents and lives with Lena, a dental nurse.
He avoids AI and leans on **Lena** and his partner Steve for anything technical.
He is calm in the slow pictures but **anxious** once robots can lift by 2031 or 2034.
His instinct is to **wait**, and a paid-off flat is his main safety plan.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because robots would reach the **lifting** work by 2031 while he waits.
whatWouldHelp: A proper **heads-up** from Brightwell about robots.
A **paid course** he can do while still working.
